title: What a pounding heart before an exam means

source.citation: Jamieson, J. P., Mendes, W. B., Blackstock, E., & Schmader, T. (2010). Turning the knots in your stomach into bows: Reappraising arousal improves performance on the GRE. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 46(1), 208-212.
source.finding: Students told before a practice test that feeling keyed up does not hurt performance, and may help it, scored higher on the maths section than a control group, and reported higher maths scores on the real exam one to three months later.
source.caveat: A small single study of adult students sitting a US graduate entrance exam. Later studies of the same idea have had uneven results. It is about ordinary pre-exam nerves only; it is not a treatment for anxiety, and the script points anyone who is struggling towards a trusted adult instead of offering advice.

scenes.narration: A pounding heart before an exam doesn't mean you're about to do badly.
Most people read those nerves as a bad sign.
In 2010, researchers told one group of students, before a practice test, that feeling keyed up could actually help.
That group scored higher on the maths section. And again on the real exam, weeks later.
Be careful with this one. It was a small study. It won't work for everyone.
And if stress feels like too much, talk to a teacher or someone you trust.
Today, before your next test, try telling yourself one thing. This is my body getting ready.
